core: working definition of a wireframe: a low-detail layout of a screen showing structure, not style (attributed to the Interaction Design Foundation)
what wireframes show: placement of content and controls, hierarchy, and spacing — each named; visual style (colors, fonts, imagery) is deliberately absent
wireframes vs prototypes: static structure vs interactive behavior (prototypes are sibling topics, referenced only)
wireframes vs mockups: structure vs visual design — the distinction stated simply
why wireframes come first: structure decisions before style decisions, on cost grounds
the levels named: low-fidelity sketches to annotated wireframes — each with one line
the honest framing: wireframes are cheap on purpose, inviting change before code exists
supporting: wireframes visualize a user path or flow, page layouts, and information hierarchy (Nielsen Norman Group)
messiness is fine and expected, especially at low fidelity; physical constraints (thick pens, time boxing) prevent obsessing over aesthetics
the four team benefits of wireframing: visualize ideas, spot opportunities and constraints, collaborate, save time and resources
the components of a well-designed wireframe: layout and structure, navigation, content hierarchy, functionality, and annotations
outOfScope: low-fidelity-prototypes and high-fidelity-prototypes — sibling topics (referenced only)
user-flows — sibling topic (referenced only, for the screens a flow passes through)
no design tools, software, or code — literacy level forbids tool tutorials
no screenshots or drawings — wireframes are described in words, never built

claims.claim: Wireframes are basic visual representations of a user interface that outline the structure and layout of a webpage or app, and they do not focus on design details like colors, fonts, or imagery (Interaction Design Foundation working definition).

Wireframes visualize a user path or flow, as well as page layouts and information hierarchy; depending on their purpose they can vary in fidelity, from quick sketches to detailed representations of the final design (Nielsen Norman Group).

A well-designed wireframe shows layout and structure (where content is arranged), navigation, content hierarchy (what is prioritized), functionality (interactive elements shown without detailing their look), and annotations (notes explaining behavior or rationale) (Interaction Design Foundation).

Wireframing is distinct from prototyping: prototyping deals more with testing interactivity (Interaction Design Foundation); Nielsen Norman Group likewise distinguishes interactive prototypes, which require a response defined for each possible user action, from static representations.

Wireframes differ from mockups: wireframes focus on the layout of a product and do not include color, images, or detailed design elements, while mockups include color, text, shapes, and other visual elements and are used to showcase a product's appearance and functionality (Interaction Design Foundation).

Prototypes are experimental, interactive models of a product that designers use to test how users and stakeholders interact with their concepts, in contrast to the static structure a wireframe shows (Interaction Design Foundation).

Wireframing early saves time and resources: when issues are identified and resolved at the wireframe stage, teams avoid expensive changes later in the process, particularly during development (Interaction Design Foundation); Nielsen Norman Group states the same economics as 'ripping up code is very expensive; ripping up a prototype is not.'

Low-fidelity wireframes are rough, simplified layouts that use placeholders for images and text, often in grayscale, to keep the focus on structure and content hierarchy; high-fidelity wireframes use accurate element sizes, actual images, and may include limited interactivity (Interaction Design Foundation).

Messiness is completely fine and expected in wireframing, especially for low-fidelity wireframes; physical constraints such as thick pens, time boxing, and limited space prevent obsessing over tiny aesthetic details, and anyone, regardless of drawing ability, can sketch a wireframe to explore possible solutions to design problems (Nielsen Norman Group).

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether wireframes may include interactivity, and how sharply the wireframe/prototype line should be drawn: the Interaction Design Foundation's wireframing page says wireframing is distinct from prototyping (which tests interactivity) yet also notes that high-fidelity wireframes 'can also include limited interactivity,' while its mockups page defines prototypes as interactive models and its wireframes definition carries no interactivity at all.
positions: Interaction Design Foundation (wireframing page): wireframing is distinct from prototyping because prototyping deals more with testing interactivity; high-fidelity wireframes can, however, include limited interactivity.
Interaction Design Foundation (mockups page): prototypes are experimental, interactive models used to test interaction; wireframes focus on layout with no color, images, or detailed design.
Nielsen Norman Group (prototype article): prototypes range from static to interactive; interactive prototypes require the designer to define a response for each possible user action.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Not a substantive conflict: all sources agree interactivity is the defining feature of prototypes and that wireframes are primarily static structure. The lesson teaches the clean working boundary — wireframes show static structure, prototypes show interactive behavior — and mentions limited interactivity only as a high-fidelity boundary case, leaving the fidelity and interactivity details to the sibling prototype topics.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft treated 'wireframe' as interchangeable with 'low-fidelity prototype' and 'mockup'; research shows the three are distinct artifacts (structure vs interactivity vs visual design) and the lesson keeps them separate.

The generated draft claimed wireframes are 'rough drawings made before any design thinking happens'; sources describe wireframing as a deliberate, structured practice grounded in user and business needs, so the lesson drops the 'before thinking' framing.
The generated draft contained no attributed working definition and no cost argument for wireframing before styling; both were written fresh from the cited sources.
correctionsNeeded: Attributed the working definition to the Interaction Design Foundation and the fidelity/flow description to Nielsen Norman Group; no unverified definitions were kept.
Named the three things wireframes show (placement, hierarchy, spacing) and stated explicitly that visual style is deliberately absent, per the sources.
Added the honest framing that wireframes are cheap on purpose — they invite change while change is free — which the draft's 'unfinished-looking' dismissal missed.
Kept low-fidelity-prototypes, high-fidelity-prototypes, visual-hierarchy, and layout strictly out of scope as sibling topics, referencing them only in relatedTopics.
Ensured all examples are original (Northwind Cycles checkout, cart sketch, floor-plan analogy) and describe wireframes in words, never drawing them.

sourceRecords.title: How to Draw a Wireframe (Even if You Can't Draw)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live via urllib on 2026-08-21. Article by Kelley Gordon, dated June 20, 2021. Supports: wireframes visualize a user path or flow, page layouts, information hierarchy, and even interactions; fidelity varies from quick sketches to detailed representations; messiness is completely fine and expected especially for low-fidelity wireframes; physical constraints (thick pens, time boxing, limited space) prevent obsessing over tiny aesthetic details; standard conventions (headers as thicker lines, body text as thinner lines, images as rectangles with an X); and the conclusion that anyone, regardless of drawing ability, can sketch a wireframe to explore design solutions. Used for verification and synthesis only; no prose reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: What are Mockups?
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Read live via urllib on 2026-08-21.
